changes.before: Append one number to a typed checkpoint list.
changes.after: Keep every item in a list as a number.

before: number[] describes an array whose elements are numbers. The brackets here belong to a type description; [3, 6] is the separate runtime array value. A number[] can be empty. It does not promise a fixed length or validate unrelated data from a file.

scores.push("9") is rejected: the array expects number elements, not numeric-looking text. const prevents replacing the scores binding, but it does not freeze the array; the successful push still mutates its contents.

Make checkpoints a number array [2, 5], then append 8. Keep all three values in order. The compiler check also tries an invalid text append, so a broadly untyped array is not equivalent to the requested number array.
after: An array is an ordered list. `number[]` means its items must be numbers. It can hold many numbers or be empty; this type does not set a fixed length.
Const stops you from giving scores a different array. It does not freeze the items inside the existing array. Adding the text `"9"` is rejected because the item type must be number.
Create checkpoints as a number array containing 2 and 5. Append 8, keeping all three numbers in order.

before.question: After the worked code, scores.push("12") is added. What does the checker report?
choices: The text argument does not match the number element type.
An array created with const cannot be changed at all.
The checker silently changes the string into a number.
before.explanation: The binding is constant, but its array is mutable. The actual problem is the string element, not const or the number of items.

after.question: Why does scores.push("12") cause a type error?
choices: The added item is text instead of a number
Const means no array items can change
TypeScript silently changes the text into a number
after.explanation: The array can change, but each new item must still be a number.
